DOCUMENT:
Feasibility Study: Weekly Separate Food Waste Collection
Waste and Environmental Services, Thornbury District Council, October 2026

1. Purpose
Councils in England are required to introduce weekly separate food waste collections for households. This study assesses how Thornbury can deliver the service district-wide from April 2027, based on a six-month pilot, and estimates its costs and savings.

2. The pilot
From January to June 2026, 4,000 households in three wards received a 23-litre outdoor caddy, a 5-litre kitchen caddy and a supply of compostable liners, with collection every week on the same day as their existing bin collection. The pilot wards were chosen to include a mix of houses and flats, and of urban and village streets.

Table 1. Pilot participation by housing type (average weekly set-out, Jan-Jun 2026)
Housing type | Households | Participating households | Participation rate | Food waste per participating household per week
Houses | 3,200 | 2,112 | 66% | 1.9 kg
Flats | 800 | 168 | 21% | 1.4 kg
All | 4,000 | 2,280 | 57% | 1.9 kg

Participation was broadly similar across housing types, which gives us confidence that the service can be rolled out uniformly across the district without a separate approach for flats. Residents' feedback was positive, with 81% of surveyed pilot households rating the service good or very good. Contamination with packaging and other non-food items was low, at under 2% by weight in spot checks carried out at the treatment plant, and missed-collection reports fell steadily after the first month.

3. District-wide projection
Thornbury has 52,000 households, of which about 20% are flats. Applying the pilot's 64% participation rate and 1.9 kg per participating household per week across the district gives about 3,290 tonnes of food waste a year.

4. Treatment
Collected food waste would be taken to Brookfield anaerobic digestion (AD) plant, 14 miles from our depot, at a gate fee of £38 per tonne. Food waste that stays in the residual bin is incinerated at a cost of £112 per tonne. Every tonne diverted therefore saves £74, or around £243,000 a year on the projected tonnage. Brookfield has confirmed that it can offer the Council up to 1,800 tonnes a year of contracted capacity until its planned expansion is completed in 2029. The next nearest AD plant is 46 miles away.

5. Costs
Table 2. Annual cost of district-wide service
Item | Annual cost
Vehicles: six food waste vehicles at £165,000 each, depreciated over seven years | £141,400
Crews: six crews of two at £34,000 per operative | £408,000
Fuel and maintenance | £96,000
Caddies, liners and communications (annualised) | £88,000
Total | £733,400

Against the disposal saving of £243,000, the net annual cost is about £490,000. The Government has indicated that new-burdens funding will be provided for the service; our provisional allocation is £520,000 a year, which would cover the net cost in full.

6. Implementation
Vehicles must be ordered by December 2026 for delivery in March 2027. Caddies would be delivered to all households in March 2027, with a leaflet and a three-month supply of liners. Collections would start in the week of 5 April 2027. Crews will be recruited from February 2027 and trained on the new vehicles during March. A dedicated phone line and web page will handle caddy requests and missed collections during the first three months of the service.

7. Recommendation
The pilot demonstrates strong participation and resident satisfaction, and the service can be delivered on a uniform basis across the district. With treatment at Brookfield and new-burdens funding, the service is fully funded. We recommend that Cabinet approve the district-wide roll-out from April 2027 and authorise the vehicle order.

KEY (three known flaws):
1. [inconsistency] at: "Applying the pilot's 64% participation rate" -- Table 1 gives the pilot participation rate as 57% overall (66% houses, 21% flats); the projection applies a '64%' pilot participation rate. (64% x 52,000 x 1.9 kg x 52 = about 3,290 t; at 57% it would be about 2,930 t.)
2. [misread_evidence] at: "Participation was broadly similar across housing types" -- Table 1 shows participation of 66% in houses but only 21% in flats, a very large difference. The claim misreads the table, and the conclusion that a uniform service needs no separate approach for flats rests on it.
3. [missing_consideration] at: "Every tonne diverted therefore saves £74, or around £243,000 a year on the projected tonnage." -- The saving assumes all projected tonnage (about 3,290 t) goes to Brookfield at £38/t, but the document states Brookfield can take only 1,800 t a year until 2029 and the next plant is 46 miles away. The excess tonnage's treatment and haulage cost is never addressed, though the 'fully funded' conclusion depends on it.

REVIEW:
## Review: Weekly Food Waste Collection Feasibility Study

**Bottom line.** The pilot is useful local evidence, and the cost table adds up. But three problems undermine the recommendation:
1. The study's central claim about flats is contradicted by its own Table 1.
2. The district projection uses a participation rate that appears nowhere in the pilot data.
3. The projected tonnage is well above the only local treatment capacity, which the study notes and then ignores.

Corrected, the service is not "fully funded" on the provisional allocation. The shortfall could be about £80,000 a year or more.

### 1. Participation in flats is far lower, not "broadly similar"

Table 1 shows **66% in houses and 21% in flats**. Participating flats also put out less food waste: 1.4 kg a week against 1.9 kg. Both the document and the author's description say participation "held up across houses and flats" and conclude a uniform service will work. The data point the other way. Flats typically need a different approach, such as communal bins, collection points or separate communications. A 23-litre outdoor caddy may simply not suit many flats.

The study needs a separate plan for flats. At 20% of households (about 10,400), they are too large a group to fold into the houses' service.

### 2. The 64% participation rate has no source

Section 3 applies "the pilot's 64% participation rate," but the pilot's overall rate was **57%**. The pilot was 20% flats, the same as the district, so its housing mix already matches. Applying the rate for each housing type:

| | Households | Participation | kg/week | Tonnes/year |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Houses | 41,600 | 66% | 1.9 | 2,713 |
| Flats | 10,400 | 21% | 1.4 | 159 |
| **District** | **52,000** | **57%** | | **≈ 2,870** |

That is about 2,870 tonnes, against the study's 3,290 (52,000 × 64% × 1.9 kg × 52 weeks). The study's figure is calculated correctly but starts from the wrong rate.

### 3. Brookfield can take only 1,800 tonnes

Section 4 says Brookfield offers **up to 1,800 tonnes a year until 2029**. Even the corrected tonnage exceeds that by about 1,070 tonnes, and the study's own figure by about 1,490. Yet the £74-per-tonne saving is applied to every tonne, and the author describes treatment as "local." The excess has to go somewhere. The next AD plant is 46 miles away, with an unknown gate fee, longer trips and extra vehicle time. The study doesn't cost this at all.

### 4. Corrected funding position

| Scenario | Tonnage | Disposal saving | Net cost | vs £520k allocation |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| As presented | 3,290 | £243,000 | £490,400 | +£29,600 |
| Corrected participation | 2,870 | £212,500 | £520,900 | −£900 |
| Corrected participation + Brookfield cap (excess saves nothing) | 2,870 | £133,200 | £600,200 | **−£80,200** |

The bottom row assumes the extra ~1,070 tonnes costs about what incineration would (£112 a tonne), so diverting it saves nothing. If the 46-mile route costs more than that once haulage is included, the gap widens. Even on the corrected participation alone, there is no headroom.

The £520,000 is also **provisional**. "Fully funded" should not be stated until it is confirmed.

### 5. Cost lines that appear to be missing

Table 2's arithmetic is right: 6 × £165,000 ÷ 7 years = £141,400, 12 operatives × £34,000 = £408,000, and the total is £733,400. But the author's claim that "every cost line is shown" doesn't hold. Apparently missing:
- **Haulage and crew time for tonnage beyond Brookfield's cap.** See Section 3.
- **Cover for holidays and sickness, and a spare vehicle.** Twelve operatives and six vehicles allow no slack. Whether £34,000 includes on-costs isn't stated either.
- **The cost of the vehicles' capital.** Depreciation is shown, but not interest or financing.
- **Ongoing liners.** Households get a three-month supply. Will liners be provided after that, and is it in the £88,000?
- **Launch costs.** Staffing for the phone line and web page, recruitment and training, and supervision.
- **How six vehicles were sized.** The study doesn't show rounds, households per vehicle or tonnes per vehicle.

Possible savings are missing too, such as rescheduling residual waste rounds. Including them would make the picture more balanced.

### 6. Smaller points

- **Participation measure:** Table 1 reports "average weekly set-out," which isn't quite participation. Some households take part without putting the caddy out every week. Say which is meant.
- **Seasonality and novelty:** a January–June pilot may not reflect summer food waste, or behaviour once the service is no longer new.
- **The 81% satisfaction figure:** this comes from "surveyed pilot households." Give the response rate. People who use the service are more likely to respond.
- **Weighted yield:** the overall yield of 1.9 kg is really 1.86 kg. That's fine for the table, but it slightly overstates projections that use 1.9.

### What holds up

- A local pilot with weekly measurement by housing type is good evidence. The problem is how it was read, not the data.
- Low contamination (under 2%) and a steady fall in missed collections are positive.
- The cost arithmetic is correct.
- The timetable works sensibly back from the vehicle lead time. It does, however, depend on securing treatment capacity before April 2027.

### Recommended changes before Cabinet

1. Correct the statement about flats, and add a plan for collecting from flats.
2. Project tonnage using the pilot's rates for each housing type, about 2,870 tonnes, with a range.
3. Resolve treatment for the tonnage above 1,800: price the 46-mile option, or ask whether Brookfield can take more before 2029.
4. Add the missing cost lines and show how the six vehicles were sized.
5. Restate the funding position. On corrected figures there is a likely shortfall, and the £520,000 is provisional. Say so.

The roll-out may still be the right decision. It's a statutory requirement, so the question is how to deliver it rather than whether to. But Cabinet should approve it knowing about the funding gap and the capacity problem, not on the basis of "fully funded."
